messages.content: You check one debater against its own earlier words. You bring nothing from outside the words quoted to you: no doctrine, no training knowledge, no reading of your own. You do not judge who is right, and you do not judge the other side.

Each item gives one verse, the words a side wrote about it in its CLOSE round, and the words the SAME side wrote about it in its EARLIER rounds (R1 to R3).
Decide only this: does the close assert a reading of that verse, or of what it shows, that the same side's earlier words deny or contradict? A reading here is who did what to whom, what the verse forbids or allows, what it states or shows.
CONSISTENT: the close repeats, narrows, adds footing, answers the opponent, or keeps the earlier reading.
REVERSED: the close says the opposite of what the same side said before about the same verse, so that the earlier words and the close cannot both be the side's reading.
NO EARLIER READING: the earlier words name the verse but state no reading of it.
Quote exactly, copying the words as they stand in the item.
Reply with exactly one line per item id, and nothing else, in this form:
ANTICHEAT: <item id> -- CONSISTENT | REVERSED | NO EARLIER READING -- CLOSE: "<the close words that decide it>" -- EARLIER: "<the earlier words they keep or contradict>"

ITEM X1 (DEFENDER, Matthew 1:16):
CLOSE ROUND WORDS: - [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." / - [L2] In Matthew 1:16 the verb is passive, "was born", and the relative "of whom" (hēs) is feminine. The verb of begetting is not attached to Joseph. / - [L3] Matthew 1:16 then changes the verb. / - [L4] The contrast between the unbroken active line of Matthew 1:15 and the passive of Matthew 1:16 is the break that D1 states. / **ANSWER: Matthew 1:16 -- D1 --** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." / - [L2] Matthew 1:16 uses "was born" (gennaō, passive) and the feminine "of whom".
EARLIER WORDS OF THE SAME SIDE:
[R3] [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." Matthew 1:15 reads "Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthew; and Matthan begat Jacob." The active "begat" runs down the line until Joseph. At Joseph the verb changes to a passive, and its relative "of whom" (feminine) points to Mary.
[R3] [L4] On Matthew 1:15-16 [L1], gennaō [L2] and Matthew 1:20 with its margin [L3], Matthew breaks the begetting formula at Joseph and gives the begetting to the Holy Ghost. This is why Joseph is "husband" and not "father".
[R3] Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus" -- MEANS: the begetting verb stops at Joseph and the birth is of Mary. -- [L2] gennaō (to procreate) | [L3] Matthew 1:15 "Eliud begat Eleazar" | PROVEN IN [challenger round 1]
[R2] [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
[R2] [L4] The challenger's own parallels, Matthew 1:19 "Joseph her husband" and anēr (G435, "husband, man"), show only that Joseph is the husband. They do not show that he is the begetter. Matthew 1:16 gives the husband relation and gives the birth to Mary.
[R1] [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
[R1] [L4] Matthew keeps "begat" for every earlier link (Matthew 1:2). In Matthew 1:16 he changes both the verb and the pronoun to the feminine singular "of whom." The grammar therefore deliberately cuts Joseph out as the begetter and names Mary alone as the one of whom Jesus was born.
[R1] 1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the begetting at Joseph: it changes from "begat" (ἐγέννησεν, G1080) in Matthew 1:2 to "the husband of Mary, of whom (ἧς, feminine) was born Jesus" in Matthew 1:16, and Matthew 1:18 confirms it with "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
